page.title: Property testing a statechart, step by step
page.description: Property test a statechart in seven steps: a world as data, properties, a seeded search, a planted bug, a shrunk counterexample and its trace, all in your browser.

hero.headline: Property testing a chart, step by step.
hero.lede: A test checks one run you thought of. A property test says what must hold for every run, generates runs from seeds, and when one breaks, shrinks it to the smallest run that still does. A chart makes this cheap: its world is a list of events, its time is simulated, and every run can be traced. The examples on this page run in your browser, on the WebAssembly build of tinyactors.

section.heading: Start with a chart.
section.p: A payment asks a service to charge a card. When no answer comes within 30 seconds it tries again, and after three attempts it gives up. It ends in paid or failed, and says which in its done data.

section.heading: Make the world data.
section.p: The chart reaches the world only through events: a charge it sends, a charged it may get back, a timeout it sends itself. So a run's world can be a plain array, one entry per charge, saying whether the service answers it. A run spawns the chart on a SimulatedClock, answers as the array says, and jumps the clock from one timeout to the next until the payment ends.
With trace on, the host's telemetry is collected and decoded into spans. Run the world [silence, answer]: the first charge times out, the second is answered.

Each row is a step the actor took, under the step that caused it. The timeout macrostep sits 30 seconds in, under the microstep whose delayed send it was. Select a row to read its transitions, the states it entered, and what it sent and cancelled.

section.heading: Say what must always hold.
section.p: A property is a function of a run that is true whatever the world did. These three come straight from the payment's description: it never charges more than three times, it gives up only after the third charge, and it is paid only when the service answered.

section.heading: Search a thousand worlds.
section.p: A generator makes a world from a seed: three to eight answers, each a yes with probability 0.4. The search runs seed after seed until a run breaks a property. A seed reproduces its world, so a failure is never lost.
Every one of those runs has three 30-second timeouts at most, and none of them waits: the simulated clock jumps.

section.heading: Plant a bug, and find it.
section.p: Change one character of the chart: retry while attempts < 4 instead of attempts < 3. The chart still compiles, still pays when the service answers, and an example-based test that answers the first charge still passes. The search finds a world where it breaks.

section.heading: Shrink it to the smallest failure.
section.p: The world the search found has answers that have nothing to do with the bug. The shrinker tries smaller worlds, one answer fewer or a yes turned into silence, and keeps any that still break a property, until none does. What is left is the failure and nothing else.

The smallest world is the empty one: the service never answers. The trace shows why that breaks the chart: three timeout steps re-enter charging, and each entry charges again, so the card is charged a fourth time, and only the fourth timeout gives up, at 120 seconds instead of 90.

section.heading: Run it in your tests.
section.p: The same module runs in Node.js and Bun. @tinyactors/wasm works there too, and @tinyactors/node has the same API. A test runs the search on every commit, and a failure names its seed, which reproduces it on any machine.

section.heading: Larger worlds, more actors.
section.p: Everything here is a pattern you write, not a library: a world as data, properties as functions, a generator, a search and a shrinker. It grows with the system under test.

item.text: Answers that come late, twice or out of order are entries in the same array, each a choice the generator makes and the shrinker can undo.
Generate the inputs to a whole system, such as the team chat's connects, posts and idle users, and state properties across actors: every online member of a room sees every post.
Spans are data too, so a property can ask how a run got there: no actor charged twice within one macrostep.
